about: Every CS Quest slide picture, keyed. A slide names a key (img); the picture lives at public/img/<key>.webp (1280x720 WebP; a picture a slide crops very narrow is captured at 2x, 2560x1440, the same layout). Decks and this manifest are checked by `npm run csq:check`; captures are made by scripts/csq-shots.js.

A threat card: a known hole in old software lets a trick letter slip in. Below it, the layer tiles, Patch Crew (updates) among them.

images.concept: a broken tablet, the only copy

Lock 5: Five Moves, open! The drill, in order, start to finish. Skill trained: run the five moves in order when something goes wrong.
Moves placed in order: tell a trusted adult fast, report and block, change the key from a clean device. One slot is left to fill.
A classmate's mailbox has been broken into. The first move placed: stop and disconnect, pass nothing on. Five slots wait.
The first move placed: stop and disconnect. Five slots wait, and below them the tiles: change the key, tell a trusted adult, save the evidence.

The Magpie's sealed note reads RSHQ, a scramble, with the Turn back and Turn forward buttons to try each shift.

Two Pim cards' clues: both postmarked Netville, today. One has small owl prints and asks for help; one has big round prints and asks for your key.

images.concept: two Pim cards, read from the top
images.alt: Lock 3: Which Pim? Two cards say From: Pim. One asks for sorting help at the front desk; one asks for your mailbox key. Postmark: Netville, today.
Three messages say they are from Pim; only one really is. Two cards: one asks for sorting help after lunch, one asks for your mailbox key.
Two Pim cards' clues: one has a hand-press postmark and owl-shaped prints; the other, the office stamp and small owl prints. Pick this card buttons.
Three messages say they are from Pim; one wears a faked trail. A card from Pim asks you to bring your mailbox key to a side gate.
Five switches worth 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1: the 4 and the 1 are on, and the total reads 5.
You take a photo and switch the tablet off. Where is the photo? In storage, kept as bits; gone forever; on the dark screen.
Read the cards: 16 off, 8 off, 4 on, 2 on, 1 off. Which number do the switches make: 6, 42 or 2?
A 5 by 5 pixel grid with rows 1 to 3 copied, beside the row codes: Row 1: 01010, Row 2: 11111, Row 3: 11111 and so on.
Five bits worth 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1: 16, 4 and 1 are on, so the bits read 10101 and the total is 21.
Eight bits make a byte, worth 128 down to 1. The 128 bit alone is on: a middle gray, 128.

images.concept: One thing, many codes: a color as three numbers
images.alt: Match the swatch: the target is 220, 90, 40, an orange. Red 220, green 100, blue 40 already looks the same.
Pick two changes that would help Ana: bigger text, a bigger Play button, captions for sounds, read the menu aloud and more.
Sol is six and cannot read yet. A box of words pops up: Save your game? Yes or No. Sol taps anywhere and loses.
Ana loves puzzle games, but small text is a blur to her. Watch Ana: which moment is she struggling?
Ana loves puzzle games, but small text is a blur to her. Watch Ana and tap the moment she struggles.
Ren plays in bright sun: changes to pick from include stronger contrast, outlines and a sun mode.
Tao tries face unlock. The makers only tested it on faces like their own, and it does not recognize Tao.
Fixes for Tao: test with people of many ages, skin tones and faces, and always offer a passcode as another way in.
The password does not work, even though you know it. The first check on the list: is caps lock on?
No sound in the headphones: two quick checks done, volume up and plugged in all the way. Next on the list: is it muted?
No wireless connection: quick checks like airplane mode take 1 minute, restarting the network box takes 5.
Ticket: it will not turn on. Hold the power button: still a black screen. Each check shows how many minutes it takes.
The printer prints nothing: the flowchart is built cheapest first: is it on, is there paper, is the job stuck, the right printer?
No internet on the laptop: before touching anything, build a flowchart of yes/no questions, cheapest first.
The headset microphone is silent: build the flowchart, and if it is still broken, swap a part.
The step counter brief: small, cheap, lasts all day. A motion sensor and a processor are in; the needs list ticks them off.
The plant waterer brief: it needs something that feels dry soil. The moisture sensor is in, and the need is ticked.
Too many parts for a step counter: the screen, wireless chip and big battery push the cost, battery and size meters up.
Three walkers tried the step counter: they could not see the count, it fell off, the battery ran flat. Pick two improvements.
Sorting cards into Hardware, what you can touch, and Software, the instructions. Five cards are sorted so far.
A Tap Travels: your finger taps, the touch sensor feels it, the processor works it out, the camera app says take a photo.
Which part takes the photo? Screen, microphone, speaker, battery, touch sensor or camera: every part has its own job.
A note to send: OAK TREE, readable by anyone. Three scrambled readings wait below; only one uses the shift of 5.
A secret word, DAOWQF, with no shift marked on the card. Only trying the wheel will show what it says.
Secret Messages: a secret word with an unknown shift. Secret message DAOWQF; your reading, DAOWQF, until the wheel turns.

images.concept: Secret codes for fun: a cipher wheel shifts each letter by the key (shift 3)
images.alt: The cipher wheel: turn the key and every letter shifts, turning a plain message into a secret one.
The cipher wheel turned to shift 3: the secret message DSSOH now reads APPLE.

images.concept: Brute force: a shift has only 25 keys, so you can try them all
images.alt: A later cipher level: with so few keys, trying every one is a real way in — for a shift cipher.
An unknown shift: turn the wheel one step at a time until DAOWQF turns into a real word.
Crack it by counting: a scrambled message, the Caesar wheel, and a button that counts how often letters appear.
Pim asks which ways to keep a secret are easy or hard to crack. The two-key lockbox: anyone can click it shut, but only the owner holds the opening key.

images.concept: A shift of 3: every letter moves the same number of places
images.alt: The wheel at work: letters are shifting along the alphabet by the key, turning plain words into code.
The shift cipher wheel turned to 3: DSSOH reads APPLE.

images.concept: Hiding is not scrambling: steganography hides a message in a picture's pixels
images.alt: Steganography: a heart hidden in a picture. Each pixel is a number, and its last bit says dot or blank, so the picture looks the same.
Hide a heart inside an ordinary picture: every pixel is a number, and its last bit, odd or even, carries the secret.
Packet Post's title screen: Pim the owl at the Netville post office. Deliver every packet. Keep every secret.

images.concept: a good spare copy, kept elsewhere
images.alt: Lock It, the spare-copy sort: a copy in the family’s online folder. A good spare copy, or not a spare copy?

images.concept: Build a passphrase: four random words, long and hard to guess
images.alt: The passphrase is taking shape: words are being picked for the mailbox key, and longer means harder to guess.
If one key opens every door, losing it opens them all: a habit card waits to be sorted, safe or risky.

images.concept: Lock it up: lock it, keep the key, keep a spare copy
images.alt: The mailbox key builder: pick words for a passphrase, the key that locks your mailbox in Packet Post.
A mailbox key built from four word tiles: volcano, giraffe, bicycle, thunder. A computer would need centuries to guess it.
A tablet holds messages and pictures. Signing out on a shared computer: does the habit protect it, or is it risky?
Sorting the mail: where you live and your mailbox key are Keep, a favorite book is Share. Next up: a joke you made up.

images.concept: share or keep: sort each fact
images.alt: Lock It, the sharing sort: the first card, where you live, waits for its tray. Share, or keep it private?
Sorted so far: the only copy on one tablet is not a spare; a family online folder, a printout and last year's copy are good spares.

images.concept: Who may know it? Only a trusted adult may know your passphrase
images.alt: Okay to Tell: a sorting round about who may hear what, where a passphrase is never fine to share.
Who may know your mailbox key? A trusted adult at home: okay to tell. Your best friend: keep it to yourself.

images.concept: the backup rule in four steps
images.alt: The backup rule in four steps: make a second copy, keep it in another place, check it opens, keep it fresh.

images.concept: Two halves of security: physical protects the machine, digital the data
images.alt: Lock It in Pro opens with the sharing sort: security starts with knowing what must be protected.

images.concept: Strong passphrases: four random words beat a short word plus a number
images.alt: The Pro mailbox key builder: a passphrase made of chosen words, different from every other account key.
Four random word tiles make the key: volcano, giraffe, bicycle, thunder. A computer would need about centuries.
Share or Shield: where you live. Good side: friends could send you a card. Risk: a stranger could turn up at your door.

images.concept: build a new key from word tiles
images.alt: The home router still has its key on a sticker anyone can read. Build a new passphrase from four word tiles.

images.concept: The padlock: details travel sealed, like an envelope, not a postcard
images.alt: The sealed route: a message travels a road marked sealed, the padlock idea played as a journey.
The shop order rides the padlock street: sealed roads wear padlocks, while the open street is shorter but read by a snoopy cat.

images.concept: Physical or digital? Sort each measure by what it protects
images.alt: Physical or Digital: the sort whose bins are the machine and the data, from locked doors to firewalls.
Physical or digital: a cable lock and a privacy screen are physical; encryption and a virus scanner are digital.

images.concept: every road meets at the center office
images.alt: Five packets for the zoo: every road on this map meets at the center office, where many hands can carry them.

images.concept: every road meets at the center office
images.alt: Break It Up, level 4: five packets for the zoo. Every road on the map meets at the Center Office before Zoo Gate.

images.concept: Meet Pim: every message must reach the right house
images.alt: Pim opens the Netville map: houses, roads and the first message waiting to be delivered.

images.concept: too big for one envelope: cut into packets
images.alt: Break it up: a picture of an apple is too big to send in one go, so the network cuts it into small numbered packets.

images.concept: Back in order: numbers put arriving packets back together
images.alt: Packets are on the roads of Netville, each carrying its number, so the far end can rebuild the message in order.
All six packets are here: 1 and 2 are back in place, and 3, 4, 5 and 6 wait to be tapped in number order.

images.concept: Too big to send: numbered packets
images.alt: Grandma's apple picture, cut into 3 numbered packets: packet 2 is on its way down the road.

images.concept: the padlock road keeps a secret sealed
images.alt: A secret birthday surprise: padlock roads run over the hill, and Pim says a snoopy cat reads every packet on the open road.

images.concept: the open road and the padlock road
images.alt: Explorer padlock level: from Pim’s Post, the padlock road climbs over Hill Office to Birthday House; the open road runs below.

images.concept: a secret goes on the padlock road
images.alt: Pim: this picture is a secret birthday surprise. On the open road a snoopy cat reads every packet; the padlock road is sealed like an envelope.

images.concept: Say got it: the receiver confirms each packet and asks for missing ones
images.alt: The delivery is under way: packets have been sent and the receiver is saying got it, watching for a gap.
Got 1, 2, 3 and 4: four mail slots are ticked, and packet 5, asked for again, is in the inbox.

images.concept: Damaged on the way? A checksum count that does not match means resend
images.alt: A later protocol level on the road: here a damaged packet must be spotted by its count and sent again.

images.concept: Damaged on the way? The checksum
images.alt: Every packet carries a dot count. Count the dots: a packet whose dots do not match what it says was damaged.
What goes wrong on this road: packet 3 never arrives, packet 2 arrives twice, they arrive mixed up. Below, the first four rule cards to pick from.

images.concept: Messages in packets: numbered, routed and rebuilt at the other end
images.alt: Rules of the Road opens: numbered packets wait at the first router, ready to travel by the shared rules.

images.concept: Rules everyone follows: a protocol is rules every computer agrees on
images.alt: A second protocol level: every router on the road follows the same rules, or no packet could be passed on.
Five packets, two lost on the way: packet 1 sits in its mail slot, and packets 2 and 4 wait in the inbox.
The second of four packets is on its way across the diamond map, two hops done and two to go.
Many roads to the school: packets can go by Hill Office or River Office, and one road will close.
Hop budget: thirteen hops for four packets. Packet 2 of 4 is on the road, and the counter reads Hops: 3 of 13.
Sealed roads wear padlocks: open roads cost one hop, but a snoopy cat reads every packet on them.
Cues found on the bank card: threatens to close, asks for the key, unknown sender. Then: Safe, Trick or Ask a trusted adult.
A card from "Your bank", unknown sender: your account is locked, send your mailbox key today. Two cues are already found.

images.concept: Trick or safe? A threat, a rush and a key request
images.alt: A card from “Your bank”, marked unknown sender: “Your account is locked.”
The prize card's cues to tap: hurry, asks for the mailbox key, a prize you never entered, says congratulations. Then Safe, Trick or Ask.

images.concept: Clues of a trick: hurry, a prize, a request for your passphrase
images.alt: The prize card's cues: hurry, only ten minutes; asks for the mailbox key; a prize you never entered; says congratulations. Then the three choices.
Cues to tap: a button that wants a tap right now; talks about coins. Then three choices: Safe, Trick, Ask a trusted adult.

images.concept: Some messages are tricks: they want you to hurry or give things away
images.alt: A prize card from Prize Team, marked unknown sender: “You won a tablet!”

images.concept: Some messages are tricks: they want you to hurry or give things away
images.alt: Cues to tap: hurry, only ten minutes; asks for the mailbox key; a prize you never entered; says congratulations. Then Safe, Trick or Ask a trusted adult.

images.concept: a stranger asks for your street
images.alt: A card from “A new friend”, marked unknown sender, asking to get together after school. Cues to tap: a personal question, from someone you have never met.

images.concept: a trick wearing a bank's name
images.alt: A trick wearing a bank's name: for your safety, it says, confirm your mailbox key and your birthday.

images.concept: Faked senders: a trick can fake its sender name, called spoofing
images.alt: A Pro trick card: the sender name looks friendly, but a faked name is exactly what spoofing means.
A card that says it is from Your bank, but carries an unknown sender badge: the name is faked.
A card from Parcel Service, marked unknown sender: “Your parcel is waiting.” Pay a small fee within two hours to get it back, with a Pay now button.
Fog covers Bolt's board: only the squares near Bolt can be seen, so no fixed list of steps could work here.
The repeat until goal program with the if / else inside it, feeling its way along the open path across a board of water.
One if / else block in the tray: if path ahead, move; else, turn left. Bolt checks and picks a side every time it runs.
A when block waits at the top of the program: when a gem is picked up, turn right, with the driving loop underneath it.
A two-question check in the tray: if wall ahead AND on a gem, pick up and turn; the spiral maze waits on the board.

images.concept: Worked example: one program, any maze
images.alt: The short sense-and-steer program beside the maze: repeat until goal, if path ahead move, else turn right.
The maze program checks at every step: repeat until goal, if path ahead move, else turn left, on a water board.

images.concept: Mission board: the big maze start
images.alt: A big walled maze with Bolt penned in one corner and the flag far away: no fixed route can be written for this.
The check reads if NOT path ahead OR on paint, turn right: one block asking two questions at once.
The Pro event program: a when block for picking up a gem, over a repeat loop whose if block picks up gems Bolt stands on.

images.concept: Done means tested: a fix is done when you run it again
images.alt: The fixed program sits in the tray: the wrong turn left has become turn right, ready to run again and be tested.

images.concept: Programs break: a bug is a mistake in a program
images.alt: The Debug Lab opens a program that does not work: Bolt waits at the start while the broken program fills the tray.
Debug Lab level 2: the flag is five squares from Bolt, but the program says repeat 6 times, move.
The broken program stepped to its turn left block: Bolt climbed three squares and now faces the wall, away from the flag.

images.concept: Step, stop, fix: step one block at a time and stop at the first surprise
images.alt: Stepping one block at a time: the first block is lit in the tray and Bolt has moved exactly one square.

images.concept: Edge cases: unusual boards break quiet assumptions
images.alt: A later Debug Lab board with an unusual layout: goals and walls sit where a program that assumes too much will fail.

images.concept: Expect bugs: a test case is one board with a known right answer
images.alt: A Pro Debug Lab board with its test tabs above it: one program must pass every board, not just this one.

images.concept: One board can hide a bug: the same program on a second test board
images.alt: The same program on Test 3, a longer hallway: Test 1 and Test 2 show a check, Test 3 a cross, and Bolt splashed into the water.

images.concept: The debug loop: a fix is done only when every test passes
images.alt: After a run, every test tab shows a mark: Test 1 and Test 2 pass, Test 3 fails, so this fix is not done yet.
The My Block named Side is defined in the tray, but nothing calls it, and Bolt has not moved: a definition alone does nothing.
Three gem steps climb like stairs to the flag, and Bolt's program tray is empty: climbing all three the long way takes a lot of blocks.
The My Block named Stair is built in the tray: move, pick up, turn right, move, turn left: one named packet of blocks.
Two My Blocks named Zig sit in the tray, and the second carries a based-on Starter blocks stamp: a remix keeps its credit.
My Block Stair is made once at the top of the program, and three call Stair blocks below it climb all three stairs.
The team's My Block Zigzag (n) heads the program, with its note: By the Robo Route team. It climbs the zigzag staircase on the board.
Three My Blocks carry plain-language notes: Sweep picks up the gems, Drop drives down the side, Home drives to the goal.

images.concept: A block with a number slot
images.alt: My Block Dash (n) repeats n moves, and the calls underneath feed it different numbers: call Dash (7), (6), (5), (4), (3).
Three named My Blocks split the job: GetGems, Climb and Cross, each defined in the tray and called in turn below.

images.concept: Worked example: three rooms, one block
images.alt: Room (steps) is defined once with steps inside it, then called three ways: call Room (1), call Room (3), call Room (2).
Bolt and the flag five squares apart in a straight row, and five move blocks in the program, one for each square.
One bracket does the work: a repeat 5 times block with a single move block inside it, and Bolt's row of five squares ahead.
A repeat 2 times bracket holds move, move, pick up, and one more move follows it: Bolt drives five squares and picks up both gems.
The repeat bracket holds turn right instead of move, so Bolt would spin on one square instead of driving anywhere.
A repeat 7 times block with one move inside crosses Bolt's whole row; written out longhand it would take seven blocks.
A repeat 3 times bracket holds a second repeat 3 times bracket with move inside it, then turn right: a loop in a loop.
A nested repeat program next to a staircase of gems: repeat 3 times outside, repeat 2 times with move and pick up inside.

images.concept: Meet Bolt: a program is a list of steps

images.concept: A plan is the steps in plain words

images.concept: Turn each plan line into blocks
images.alt: The finished program for the plan level fills the tray: twenty-one blocks that follow the plan lines in order.
Halfway up the gem column, Bolt's counter pill reads count = 2: two gems picked up, two counted, and the change block is lit.
Three gems lie on the way to a door that opens at count = 3, and the program sets count to 0 before the loop.
Bolt's row holds three gems, then a door, then the flag; the door's counter reads count = 3 and the starter program counts.
The program names its box: set count to 0, then repeat 5 times move, pick up, and change count by 1, beside the gem column.
Bolt stands by the door with the counter strip reading steps = 2: set steps to 4 started it, and change steps by -1 ticks it down.

images.concept: Hold a value (the starter names it x)
images.alt: The starter program counts with a box named x: set x to 0, change x by 1. The value works, but the name says nothing.
The same counting program with the box named count: set count to 0 and change count by 1 read like a sentence.
A flag variable in the tray: set hasKey to Off at the start, and set hasKey to On inside the if block that picks the key up.
Two rounds into repeat 6, the watch strip reads steps = 4: set steps to 6 started it, and each change steps by -1 brings it down.
